prompt: Match each metric to its type.
Messages waiting in a queue right now: counter or gauge?

choices.text: Gauge
choices.why: Right: how many there are now, up and down.

choices.text: Counter, because messages are counted
choices.why: Counting is not the test; going down is.

choices.text: Histogram, because messages wait different times
choices.why: The waiting time would be a histogram; the number waiting is not.

choices.text: Either, as long as it ends in `_total`
choices.why: `_total` marks a counter, and a queue depth is not one.

prompt: `rate(process_cpu_seconds_total[1m])` returned 0.0193. What percentage of one processor core is the storefront using, to the nearest whole number?
A team reports "requests so far" as a gauge and graphs `rate()` of it. What goes wrong at the first restart?

choices.text: Nothing: a gauge and a counter are stored the same way
choices.why: Storage is the same; the meaning `rate()` assumes is not.

choices.text: The value drops, and the graph is wrong around it
choices.why: Right: declared as a gauge, the drop is not handled as a reset, and the series cannot be summed across instances either.

choices.text: Prometheus refuses to scrape a gauge that only grows
choices.why: It scrapes whatever it is given.

choices.text: The `_created` line is missing, so the rate is zero
choices.why: `_created` does not decide the rate.

prompt: The buckets read `le="0.025"` 16 and `le="0.05"` 270. How many checkouts took between 25 and 50 ms?

choices.why: That bucket includes the 16 below it.
Buckets are not added together.
Right: 270 minus 16.
Those are the ones at or under 25 ms.

prompt: With every checkout taking about 0.33 s, the median came back as 0.375. Where did 0.375 come from?

choices.text: A few slow checkouts pulled the median up
choices.why: All took about the same; a median is not pulled by outliers.

choices.text: The 300 ms fault plus 75 ms of network
choices.why: The number is the bucket's, not a sum of delays.

choices.text: The middle of the 0.25 to 0.5 bucket, which held them all
choices.why: Right. With nothing finer to read, interpolation lands in the middle.

choices.text: `rate()` rounded to the nearest eighth
choices.why: No such rounding exists.

prompt: The target is "checkouts under 300 ms". What makes the histogram answer that exactly?

choices.text: More traffic, so interpolation averages out
choices.why: More traffic does not move bucket boundaries.

choices.text: A higher percentile, like the 99.9th
choices.why: A higher percentile is still interpolated.

choices.text: A bucket boundary at 0.3
choices.why: Right: then "under 0.3" is a bucket's count.

choices.text: A summary instead of a histogram
choices.why: The Python client's summary has no quantiles at all.

prompt: A histogram answers exactly the share of observations below a value that is a bucket ___.
What did the Python client's summary publish after three observations?

choices.text: A count, a sum and a created time
choices.why: Right: no quantiles.

choices.text: The three observations, one per line
choices.why: Observations are never published.

choices.text: The 50th, 90th and 99th percentiles of the three
choices.why: Clients in other languages publish those; Python's does not.

choices.text: Buckets, like a histogram
choices.why: A summary has no buckets.

prompt: Three copies of a service each publish a 99th percentile from a summary. How do you get the 99th percentile of all three together?

choices.text: Average the three numbers
choices.why: An average of percentiles is not a percentile.

choices.text: Take the largest of the three
choices.why: That is an upper bound at best, and often far off.

choices.text: You cannot, from those numbers
choices.why: Right. Histogram buckets can be summed; percentiles cannot.

choices.text: Weight each by its request count
choices.why: Weighting does not recover the distribution.

prompt: The storefront counts requests by route, method and status code. What is one series?

choices.text: One request
choices.why: Requests increment series; they are not series.

choices.text: One label
choices.why: A label alone is not a series.

choices.text: One combination of label values
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: One scrape
choices.why: A scrape reads every series.

prompt: A metric has labels route (3 values), method (2) and code (4). At most how many series can it have on one instance?
Counted by plan, the logins made three series, but the head grew by 22. Where did the rest come from?
hint: What does a new target bring?

choices.text: From other users logging in at the same time
choices.why: The experiment counts its own fixed 20000.

choices.text: From `_created` gauges and the new target's own metrics
choices.why: Right: `up`, scrape statistics and the process metrics came too.

choices.text: From Prometheus keeping three copies of every series for safety
choices.why: It keeps one.

choices.text: From the logins of the previous experiment, still in memory
choices.why: This was the first one.

prompt: What is a label's cardinality?

choices.text: How long its name is
choices.why: Length does not matter.

choices.text: How many distinct values it takes
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: How often it is scraped
choices.why: Labels are not scraped on their own.

choices.text: How many metrics use it
choices.why: That is a different count.

prompt: With logins counted by user, Prometheus went from 96 MB to 158 MB. How many megabytes did the one label cost?
Which of these are bad metric labels? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `request_id`
choices.why: Yes: one series per request.

choices.text: `email`
choices.why: Yes: one per customer, and personal data too.

choices.text: `route`, with the template `/orders/{id}`
choices.why: A template is a small known set.

choices.text: `code`
choices.why: A handful of status codes.

choices.text: `url`, with the full query string
choices.why: Yes: every distinct URL is a series.

prompt: Where should the user id of a slow login go, if not in a metric label?

choices.text: Nowhere: user ids must never be recorded
choices.why: An opaque id is fine in a span; personal data like an e-mail is not.

choices.text: In a separate metric just for user ids
choices.why: That is the same cardinality with a different name.

choices.text: On the login's span
choices.why: Right: stored once, whatever its value.

choices.text: In the metric's `# HELP` line
choices.why: HELP describes the metric, not a request.

prompt: Memory climbs and you do not know which metric. Which request names the culprit fastest?
hint: Prometheus keeps statistics about its head.

choices.text: `up`, to see which target is new
choices.why: The culprit may be an old target with a new label.

choices.text: The TSDB status API
choices.why: Right: series per metric, values per label.

choices.text: `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` over a week
choices.why: It says that it grew, not what grew.

choices.text: Restarting Prometheus and watching it fill again
choices.why: Slow, and loses the evidence.

prompt: Why look at the TSDB status page when nothing is wrong?

choices.text: To know the normal numbers, so a jump stands out
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It resets the counters when visited
choices.why: Visiting changes nothing.

choices.text: Prometheus drops series nobody has viewed
choices.why: It keeps them all.

choices.text: It is the only place series can be deleted
choices.why: It is a read-only view.

prompt: After the drop rule, 20016 samples per scrape survived instead of about 16. Why?

choices.text: The rule only applies after Prometheus restarts
choices.why: It was reloaded, and `_total` disappeared.

choices.text: It dropped only `demo_logins_total`, and the `_created` series came through
choices.why: Right. A rule is as complete as its regular expression.

choices.text: Relabelling cannot drop more than half a scrape
choices.why: No such limit.

choices.text: The logins container sent the series twice
choices.why: Each series is sent once per scrape.

prompt: Where does the real fix for a high-cardinality label belong?
hint: The relabel rule is a stopgap.

choices.text: In the managed service's pricing plan
choices.why: A bigger plan pays for the problem.

choices.text: In more memory for Prometheus
choices.why: That postpones it.

choices.text: In the instrumentation
choices.why: Right: count by plan, put the user on the span.

choices.text: In a shorter retention
choices.why: Active series cost memory whatever the retention.

prompt: Put the response to a cardinality explosion in a sensible order.
items: Find the metric and label in the TSDB status
Drop the metric at the scrape with a relabel rule
Change the instrumentation to a small set of values
Remove the relabel rule once the new version is everywhere
